ranking.rationale: Age is a broadly stable predictor of commute time across states, capturing life-stage differences in job type, family constraints, and commuting patterns without relying on geography-specific artifacts.
Commute mode is directly tied to travel time and tends to generalize across states better than geography or highly state-specific codes.

Educational attainment is a strong, broadly stable predictor of commute/travel time through job type, work schedule, and residential sorting, while being less geography-specific than location codes or occupation details.

Income-to-poverty ratio is a stable socioeconomic predictor of commute patterns and travel time, adding broad signal beyond age, education, and commute mode without directly encoding geography or state-specific artifacts.

Occupation is strongly predictive of commute time through job type, work schedule, and typical workplace location, and it should generalize better across states than geography-coded variables. It adds substantial stable signal beyond age, commute mode, education, and income.
Marital status is a stable socioeconomic and household-structure signal that can improve travel-time prediction across states without directly encoding geography or domain-specific artifacts.

Disability is a broadly meaningful, state-stable predictor of commute/travel-time constraints and labor-market access, adding signal beyond age, education, occupation, and work commute without relying on geography or state-specific artifacts.
Sex is a broadly stable individual attribute that can still add modest predictive signal for commute/travel-time patterns without leaking geography or state-specific artifacts.

Mobility status one year ago is plausibly predictive of commute time through recent residential/work-location changes and moving-related commuting patterns, while being less directly tied to state identity than geographic codes and more likely to generalize across states than race or household-structure shortcuts.

Citizenship adds stable, semantically meaningful information about mobility, labor-market access, and commuting patterns that can generalize across states better than geography codes or brittle household proxies.

Household relationship can still add stable signal about commuting patterns and household structure without directly encoding state-specific geography; it is generally more transferable than race or geographic identifiers and more informative than parent-employment status for this mostly adult travel-time task.

Race can add some stable signal for commuting patterns and travel time through persistent structural differences, while being less directly domain-leaky than geographic identifiers. The remaining options are either clearly geographic shortcuts (ST, PUMA, POWPUMA) or weak/less relevant for this adult travel-time task (ESP).

Employment status of parents can still carry stable socioeconomic and household-structure signal for travel time, while the remaining options are direct geographic identifiers that are much more likely to encode state- or locality-specific artifacts and hurt OOD generalization.
Place-of-work PUMA can add commuting-pattern signal that is more directly related to travel time than state or residence geography, while still being less purely domain-identifying than ST or PUMA.

PUMA can still add some within-state local commuting structure and neighborhood context that may help predict travel time, while ST is a direct domain identifier and more likely to encode state-specific artifacts that hurt OOD stability.

State is the strongest remaining signal for travel-time differences because commuting patterns, transit access, urbanization, and regional infrastructure vary systematically across states; although it can encode domain shift, it adds substantial predictive value beyond the already selected individual and household features.
